12. HAZARD TO LIFE
Introduction
12.1.1.1 This section of the EIA presents the analysis and findings of the hazard to life
assessment undertaken for the Project.
12.1.1.2 In accordance with Section 3.5.12 of the EIA Study Brief (ESB-373/2025), a hazard
to life assessment should be conducted to evaluate the risks associated with the
use, transport and storage of explosives during construction of the Project.
12.1.1.3 Drill-and-blast excavation method will be adopted for the construction of tunnels for
this Project. In addition, a magazine, to be constructed by the MTRC for Northern
Link Project, will be handed over for the use of this Project to secure the explosive
supply, allowing flexible blasting time and multiple faces under different excavation
sequence to give a maximum tunnel production rate. The hazard to life assessment
presented in this section addressed the following:
• Overnight storage of explosives in temporary magazine;
• Transport of explosives from the magazine to the explosives unloading points;
• Transport of explosives from explosives unloading points to the blast faces; and
• Use of explosives during the construction of the tunnels.
Legislation Requirements and Evaluation Criteria
12.2.1.1 The key legislation and guidelines that are considered relevant to the hazard to life
assessment for the Project are as follows:
• Technical Memorandum on Environmental Impact Assessment Process (EIAO-
TM);
• Dangerous Goods Ordinance (Cap. 295); and
• The EIA Study Brief (ESB-373/2025) Section 3.5.12 and Appendix K.
Technical Memorandum on Environmental Impact Assessment Process
(EIAO-TM)
12.2.2.1 Annex 4 of the EIAO-TM specifies the individual and societal risk guidelines.
12.2.2.2 Individual risk (IR) is the predicted increase in the chance of fatality per year to an
individual due to a potential hazard. The individual risk guidelines require that the
maximum level of off-site IR should not exceed 1 in 100,000 per year, i.e. 1×10-5
per year.
12.2.2.3 Societal risk expresses the risks to the whole population. The Hong Kong Risk
Guidelines (HKRG) is presented graphically in Diagram 12-1. It is expressed in
terms of lines plotting the frequency (F) of N or more deaths in the off-site population

Bulk Emulsion Precursor
12.3.4.5 Bulk emulsion has a similar composition to cartridged emulsion except that it does
not contain aluminium. The bulk emulsion precursor has a density of 1.38-1.40 g/cc.
Prior to sensitisation, it is not considered as an explosive, and is classified as UN
5.1 oxidising substance which yields oxygen readily to stimulate the combustion of
other materials.
12.3.4.6 Before sensitisation, bulk emulsion precursor is stable under normal conditions and
there is no major fire hazard. The oxidising properties of bulk emulsion precursor
are considered the major hazard of it, which can cause irritation to eyes and skin.
Explosion of bulk emulsion precursor is only possible under prolonged fire,
supersonic shock or very high energy projectile impact.
12.3.4.7 Due to its stability under normal conditions, the storage and transport of bulk
emulsion precursor will not be further considered in this QRA.
Blasting Explosives
12.3.4.8 Bulk emulsion will be used as the main blasting explosives to excavate rock by rock
blasting. It will be manufactured on-site and requires the use of initiating explosives.
12.3.4.9 The bulk emulsion precursor will be sensitised at the blasting site by adding a
gassing solution which contains sodium nitrate.
12.3.4.10 The gassing solution will be injected into the bulk emulsion precursor to reduce the
density to 0.8-1.1 g/cc at the discharge end of the loading hose. This produces
nitrogen gas bubbles that aid the propagation of the detonation wave, and the
emulsion is said sensitised. The sensitised emulsion can then be detonated with
the assistance of a cartridged emulsion / small booster and a detonator.
12.3.4.11 The bulk emulsion, once being gassed, is classified as UN 1.1D explosive or S1DG.
The bulk emulsion blasting explosives once it is mixed should be pumped into and
completely fill the blast hole.

Charges and Delays
12.3.5.1 In order to facilitate a smooth blasting, perimeter holes will be lightly charged, using
either detonating cords or string loading of emulsion. Detonating cords must be
delivered to site as Schedule 1 Dangerous Goods (S1DG) (explosives). The typical
quantity used per perimeter blasthole is two strips of 40g per meter detonating cord.
12.3.5.2 Each blasthole will also require a detonator, and it is also delivered to site as S1DG
(explosives). Each detonator typically contains up to 1g of explosive as the base
charge. A small quantity of detonators or light (5g per meter) detonating cord is
also required to complete the hook-up of all the individual blasthole detonators.
12.3.5.3 The cartridged emulsion / boosters, detonating cord and detonators would need to
be delivered to site as S1DG (explosives). These are commonly all called packaged
explosives, to distinguish them from bulk emulsion, which is not a S1DG (explosives)

12.3.5.4 It is assumed that where the MIC is restricted to less than 1 TNT eqv. kg, cartridges
initiated by electronic detonators would be selected to provide additional confidence

12.3.5.5 Bulk emulsion explosives, which will only being sensitised on site, will be adopted

receiver which the allowable chargeweight is low.
12.3.5.6 A majority of drill-and-blast tunnels for the Project are expected to be excavated
using bulk emulsion to be initiated by non-electric detonators. It is assumed in this
assessment that the MIC for any single detonation will be 10 TNT eqv. kg. for all

The Need of a Magazine
12.3.6.4 Daily blasting will be anticipated for tunnel excavation throughout the project. The
supply of explosives for blasting relies on a daily delivery from Mines Division. This
delivery is typically made available between 11am and 2pm each day, and the
explosives are expected to be used immediately, limiting to a single blast each day
during the afternoon. In order to expedite the tunnel excavation with minimised idle
time in the blast cycle and mitigate the potential risk of missing out the explosives
delivery by Mines Division due to unforeseen site conditions e.g. extra time for
temporary support, machine malfunction, an explosive magazine with storage
capacity of 800 TNT eqv. kg at the magazine site is required to allow flexible blasting
time.
12.3.6.5 It shall be noted there may be other situations which might require additional
explosives quantities, such as areas of low Maximum Instantaneous Charge (MIC),
less than 1 TNT eqv. kg allowable MIC, or additional blasting for connecting
passages, niches etc. which are in addition to the regular blast faces for tunnels.
Selection of Magazine Site
12.3.6.6 Following the searches for potential magazine sites for previous Drill-&-Blast tunnel
projects, a further review has been carried out for the Project. Six potential
magazine sites have been identified, including three previously used magazine
sites (Tai Shu Ha, So Kwun Wat and Sha Tin Cavern magazine site) for the Hong
Kong Section of Guangzhou – Shenzhen – Hong Kong Express Rail Link (XRL),
CEDD Liangtang projects and Drainage Services Department Shatin Cavern
project, three other potential magazine sites at Ngau Kwu Leng Trail, Firing Range
and Lam Tei Quarry. Appendix 12.9 summarizes the potential magazine site
selection.
12.3.6.7 Tai Shu Ha (Yuen Long) has been chosen as the proposed temporary magazine
site due to its better suitability in terms of land availability, relatively less public
disturbance, remote location, and compliance with established design standard. An
additional benefit of selecting this location is its close proximity to the proposed
blasting sites, which reduces transportation distance and time for delivering
explosives to the construction site.
12.3.6.8 Temporary explosive magazine site at Tai Shu Ha (Yuen Long) is anticipated to be
utilized by NOL project before it can be used by NMH project. Liaison with NOL
project for the handover of magazine site is required.

leading to fatalities with full justification by reviewing historical accident data and
previous similar projects.
iv. Consequence Analysis: Analyse the consequences of the identified hazardous
scenarios.
v. Risk Integration and Evaluation: Evaluate the risks associated with the identified
hazardous scenarios. The evaluated risks will be compared with the HKRG to
determine their acceptability. Where necessary, risk mitigation measures will
be identified and assessed to comply with the ALARP principle used in the
HKRG.

Hazard Properties of Emulsion Types Explosives
12.6.2.6 Typical emulsion explosives contain more than 78% Ammonium Nitrate (AN), which
is considered as a powerful oxidizing agent. Friction or impact found in normal
handling will not trigger initiation of emulsion based explosives. However, heat and
confinement or severe shock (e.g. from other explosion) can cause explosion of
them. The sensitivity of AN based explosives to deflagration or detonation is
proportional to temperatures.
12.6.2.7 There are two broad categories of emulsions:
• Packaged emulsion (sensitized); and
• Bulk emulsion precursor (void-free liquid)
12.6.2.8 Cartridged emulsions are sensitized by either adding gassing solution or plastic
microspheres at the point of manufacture in ordered to fulfil their intended function
before transportation. Bulk emulsions are sensitized at the point of use on-sites.
The difference in chemical properties between these two categories of emulsion is
hence mainly due to the timing of presence of sensitizer.
12.6.2.9 Matrix or bulk emulsion (no voids) is not shock-sensitive since there is no known
mechanism for the shock front to propagate. Also, heating a void-free liquid
requires a very high pressure.
12.6.2.10 A local stimulus generating ‘hot spots’, such as sparks, friction, impact, static
electricity, extreme ambient temperature, does not cause packaged emulsions
(sensitized) to readily deflagrate under normal atmospheric conditions. To generate
a deflagration which may subsequently transit to a detonation, a pressure in excess
of 5 bars above atmospheric pressure is additionally required in the “deflagration
mass”.
12.6.2.11 The behaviour of packaged emulsion following a shock or thermal stimulus is
discussed in the following sections.
Accidental Packed Emulsion Initiation by Fire
12.6.3.1 Pools of molten AN may be formed in a fire. They may explode particularly if they
are contaminated with other materials such as copper. AN may also melt and
decompose with a release of toxic fumes which are mainly oxides of nitrogen. AN’s
sensitivity to local stimuli increases when the temperature is beyond 140˚C [3] or in
its molten form.

12.6.3.2 When the explosives are subjected to fire engulfment, many of them ignite and burn,
deflagrate, and even detonate in some cases. These were indicated by a number
of tests. The time for an explosive to ignite is dependent on its physical
characteristics and chemical composition.
12.6.3.3 Cartridged emulsions are generally considered less sensitive to fire engulfment as
a mean of initiation due to their high water content. However, the water content of
the emulsion will be driven off when exposed to heat or fire. If the energy level of
the heat is high enough, of long duration and with confinement pressure increases,
cartridge emulsions may initiate.
12.6.3.4 The temperature of any reactive medium will be clearly raised by a fire surrounding
the explosive load and enable evaporation of components (e.g. water). The rate at
which evaporation occurs is dependent on the extent of fire and the heat transfer
based on the design of the cargo container wall. The external part of the container
wall will be heated directly with the flame. Heat will eventually be transferred to the
explosive loads.
12.6.3.5 The transport accident statistics for ANFO indicate a minimum time to deflagration
is about 30 minutes. Emulsions are considered more difficult to be initiated than
ANFO as they contain higher water content.
12.6.3.6 The consequences of an accidental explosion due to thermal stimulus could be a
thermal explosion or detonation or sometimes a combination of the two.
Accidental Packed Emulsion Initiation by Means Other Than Fire
12.6.4.1 There are commonly two distinct groups of non-fire initiation mechanisms:
mechanical and electrical energy. Both shock and friction initiation are classified
as mechanical as in most accidental situations, they are difficult to be distinguished.
It has been recorded that some non-emulsion type explosives can initiate (in the
absence of piercing) mechanically at an impact velocity as low as 15 m/s. If the
explosives are pierced, it is likely that the required velocity will be far less than
15m/s. It is because localised heat generation resulting from frictional rubbing
between layers of explosives, and is regarded as ‘stab-initiation’.
12.6.4.2 However, as demonstrated by the bullet impact test from a high velocity projectile,
cartridged emulsions are insensitive to initiation by impact. According to the bullet
impact test, it requires at least 10 times the energy level of that required to detonate
nitroglycerine (NG) based explosives.
12.6.4.3 There are minimum ignition energy levels for all explosives, above which initiation
will occur. Minimum ignition energy levels typically range between 0.015J and
1.26J.
12.6.4.4 The required ignition energy level of most explosives, including cartridged
emulsions, is far exceeded by contact with mains electricity. The energy levels
possible from batteries or alternators fitted to motor vehicles, or that due to static
build-up on clothing are typically less than that required to initiate most commercial
explosives (e.g. 0.02J or less). Therefore, only very sensitive explosives are likely
to be ignited from these electrical energy sources and electrical energy is not a
possible mean of initiation for the types of explosives used in this Project.

Boulder Fall Consequence
12.8.4.5 The estimation of boulder fall consequence is based on the methodology introduced
in the GEO Report No.81 [12]. The probability of a falling rock of greater than
150mm diameter that hit a moving vehicle can be presented by the fraction of the
road occupied by the vehicle, which is defined as the probability of spatial impact
given a rock fall.
12.8.4.6 The probability of a moving vehicle hit by a falling rock with a diameter greater than
150mm is based on fraction of the road occupied by the vehicle which is defined as:
P(S:H) = (AADT x Length of the vehicle) / (average vehicle speed x 24,000)
Where
AADT is the annual average daily traffic (i.e. the number of vehicles per day);
Length of the vehicle is assumed to be 5m;
Average vehicle speed is assumed to be 30 miles/hr (i.e. 48 km/hr); and
Conversion factor for units is 24,000.
12.8.4.7 The above equation is modified to calculate the probability of a falling rock of greater
than 150mm diameter that hit a pedestrian as below:
P(S:H) = (Number of pedestrians per day x Width of a person)/ (average walking speed
x 24,000)
Where
Number of pedestrians per day is obtained by site survey;
Width of a person is assumed to be 1 m;
Average walking speed is assumed to be 5 km/hr; and
Conversion factor for units is 24,000.
12.8.4.8 The probability that a rock hits a vehicle is then given by:
P(S) = 1-{1-P(S:H)}Nrf
Where
Nrf is the frequency of rock fall per year.
12.8.4.9 The probability of loss of life of an occupant given a vehicle is hit by a rock is
assumed as 0.2 [12]. Size of the rock, number of occupants inside the vehicle and
the protection of the vehicle are already considered in this probability.

12.11.2.2 In this Project, CBA, if needed, would be applied by calculating the implied cost of

12.11.2.3 ICAF is a measure of the cost per life saved over the lifetime of the project due

value of life to determine whether a mitigation measure is reasonably practicable to
implement, i.e. if ICAF is less than the value of life, then the mitigation measure
should be implemented. In this study the value of life is taken as HK$33M, which
is the same figure as used in previous risk assessment reports including QRA of
STC STW EIA. An aversion factor is taken as 20 and the adjusted value of life
using this aversion factor is HK$660M. This is the value to measure how much the
society is willing to invest to prevent a fatality, where there is potential for an event
to cause multiple fatalities.

(MJE) is estimated for determining whether a mitigation measure is justifiable. The
